notes: \cpara{Opens with the Pythagoreans, whose school is said to have kept its teachings secret. The \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} finds secrecy attested for some doctrines, and says that the idea that all of Pythagoras' teachings were secret ``was used in the later tradition to explain the lack of Pythagorean writings''.}

\cpara{Recalls the author's earlier view that science is public by definition. The summary matches ``Scientific Evidence, Legal Evidence, Rational Evidence'' (2007), where the open-access idea was offered with ``Perhaps''.}
\cpara{States the other vision: science hidden and guarded by robed cults, so that more people will study it.}
\cpara{States the problem the proposal answers: science is open, and few study it.}
\cpara{Brings in the scarcity effect from the previous day's post, ``Scarcity,'' and adds that it is ``especially strong with information.''}

\clogic{The studies of information in ``Scarcity'' (a banned speech, testimony jurors were told to ignore, exclusive news of a beef shortage) show forbidden or exclusive information gaining influence. None of them measures how hard people try to obtain information; the studies of effort there concern a toy and a detergent.}
\cpara{The post's central claim, offered with ``I think'' and no evidence: people take freely available information to be unimportant, and prefer secret gibberish to open science.}
\cpara{Compares science to the letter in Poe's story, hidden by being left in plain view.}

\cpara{Says openness hides science from all but the initiated; ``a hundred times more effectively'' is a figure of speech. The joke in the parenthesis: walking on hot coals is survivable partly because embers conduct heat poorly, so the trial's ``secret'' is insulation.}
\cpara{Imagines the effect of hidden science: people desperate to get in, the more so on seeing what advanced physicists can do.}
\cpara{Imagines rival cults forced to compete with a secret science that can show results.}
\cpara{Returns to the Pythagoreans, as a joke; see the note on the first paragraph.}

\cpara{Raises the objection that science is already hard to enter, so the scarcity effect should already apply. The answer is that scarcity works on appearances: ``the public thinks that science is freely available.'' The post treats difficulty only as a possible source of scarcity, not as a reason in itself why people do not study something.}
\cpara{Illustrates the claim: nobody looks at a light bulb with awe, so neither do you, though you do not know how it works.}
\cpara{Says any object becomes magical if everyone treats it so, and that being allowed to know removes the need to learn.}
\cpara{Concedes that science's real initiations leave scientists satisfied; the problem is that few people start.}

\cpara{Imagines Darwin's theory taught after a costly ceremony: the initiate would be satisfied, and would laugh at creationists. The satisfaction has experimental support. Aronson and Mills (1959) found that women who read embarrassing material to join a discussion group rated the group ``significantly more attractive'' than women who had a mild initiation or none.}
\cpara{Adds that such a school might be more fun, especially if initiates had to put the evidence together themselves. ``Initiation Ceremony,'' posted the same day, stages a ceremony of this kind.}
\cpara{Applies the test of ``Is Humanism A Religion-Substitute?'', posted two days earlier: a ritual is fine if it would still make sense in a world that never had religion.}
\cpara{Disclaims the proposal, for now, because efficiency matters in fields such as medical research, and ends on a joke about selling a secret for \$100,000.}

\cpara{States the real purpose: to imagine science as secret so as not to undervalue it, and to trust no group in robes and masks ``unless they also show you the data.'' The advice is an exercise of imagination; the post gives no evidence that it changes how much anyone values science.}
\cpara{Says the hunger for secret knowledge is not a fault, since there are real deep truths, such as quantum mechanics; the fault is presenting them as mundane.}
\cpara{States as certain, and without evidence, that a hunger for secret knowledge not met by true beliefs will be met by false ones.}

\cpara{Concedes that science ``isn't really free'': courses and textbooks cost money. With the difficulty granted earlier, the post has two plain reasons why few people study science, and gives no evidence that favors its own explanation, the image problem, over them.}
\cpara{Ends with the aim: science that is open in fact and valued as if it were secret.}
